degree_six_research_response.response:
Yes. The coefficient  $5/62$  is sharp for the specified selections, even in two-connected bipartite graphs with minimum degree  $2$  and maximum degree  $6$ . The crucial cap has a direct combinatorial proof:
$$\boxed{\beta_2(H-e)=\beta_2(H)=35.}$$
The cyclic construction then gives, for every integer  $k\ge1$ ,
$$|V(G_k)|=62k,\qquad |S_k|=40k,\qquad
\beta_2(G_k)=35k,$$
so that
$$|S_k|-\beta_2(G_k)=5k=\frac{5}{62}|V(G_k)|.$$
The proof below does not use the reported DP or any finite search. The all- $k$  argument is sound. There is one minor wording correction: the witness subgraph consisting of offsets  $2,3$  is two-regular, namely a Hamiltonian cycle; the offsets- $0,1,2,3$  backbone is four-regular.1. Notation and the witness graphWrite  $H^-=H-e$ . Reindex each wing by  $j\in\mathbb Z/5\mathbb Z$ , using superscripts  $L,R$ ; thus  $a_j^R$  denotes the original  $a_{j+5}$ , and similarly for the other vertices.Each six-vertex block is the path
$$a_j-x_j-c_j-y_j-b_j-i_j.$$
The cross-witness adjacencies are
$$\begin{aligned}
N(a_j^L)\cap W_R
&=\{a_j^R,b_j^R,a_{j+1}^R,b_{j+1}^R,a_{j+2}^R\},\\
N(b_j^L)\cap W_R
&=\{b_j^R,a_{j+1}^R,b_{j+1}^R,a_{j+2}^R\},
\end{aligned}                                                    \tag{1}$$
except that  $b_0^Lb_0^R$  is deleted in  $H^-$ .Fix an arbitrary dissociation set  $D$  of  $H^-$ . Thus every vertex of  $H^-[D]$  has degree at most one. All definitions below refer to this fixed  $D$ .A selected witness is cross-saturated if it has a selected witness neighbour in the opposite wing. Such a witness cannot have any further selected neighbour.Call a block:occupied if at least one of its two witnesses  $a,b$  is selected;good if it is occupied and its  $b$ -witness is not cross-saturated;full and cross-free if both witnesses are selected and neither is cross-saturated.In particular, every selected  $b$ -witness belonging to a good block has no selected cross neighbour. A good block may contain only its  $a$ -witness, and that  $a$ -witness may be cross-saturated.For a wing  $T\in\{L,R\}$ , let  $o_T,g_T,f_T$  count its occupied, good, and full cross-free blocks, respectively.The central structural fact is that the witness pairs in
$$L_j,\ R_{j+1}$$
are joined by a complete  $K_{2,2}$ . None of these edges is the deleted edge.2. Three elementary local boundsThese bounds account for all local choices, including the single total neighbour capacity of a selected  $u$ .2.1. A six-vertex block contributes at most three plus its good-block indicatorFor every block  $B$ ,
$$|D\cap B|\le 3+\mathbf 1_{\{B\text{ good}\}}.             \tag{2}$$
There are three cases.If neither witness is selected, the selected vertices among  $x,c,y$  contribute at most two, because they induce a  $P_3$ , and  $i$  contributes at most one. The total is at most three.If  $b$  is cross-saturated, neither  $y$  nor  $i$  can be selected. The remaining vertices  $a,x,c$  induce a  $P_3$ , so they contribute at most two; together with  $b$ , the total is again at most three.In every other occupied block, the block is good. Its  $P_6$  contributes at most four: partition it into the two paths
$$\{a,x,c\},\qquad \{y,b,i\},$$
each of which contributes at most two.Consequently, when a wing’s  $u$ -vertex is absent,
$$|D\cap V_T|\le 15+g_T.                                  \tag{3}$$
2.2. A wing whose  $u$ -vertex is selected contributes at most  $12+o_T+f_T$ Suppose  $u_T\in D$ . Since  $u_T$  is adjacent to all five  $i$ -vertices,
$$\bigl|D\cap\{i_0^T,\ldots,i_4^T\}\bigr|\le1.              \tag{4}$$
This is one capacity shared across the entire wing.Within a block, first omit  $i$  and consider the path
$$a-x-c-y-b.$$
Its contribution is at most
$$2+\mathbf 1_{\{\text{occupied}\}}
  +\mathbf 1_{\{\text{full and cross-free}\}}.            \tag{5}$$
Indeed:If neither witness is selected, only the  $P_3$  on  $x,c,y$  remains, giving at most two.If exactly one witness is selected, the available four-vertex path gives at most three.If both witnesses are selected but  $a$  is cross-saturated, then  $x\notin D$ , and the contribution is at most  $1+\beta_2(P_3)=3$ .If both witnesses are selected but  $b$  is cross-saturated, then  $y\notin D$ , with the same bound.If both witnesses are selected and neither is cross-saturated, the five-vertex path gives at most four.Summing (5), then adding the selected  $u_T$  and at most one selected  $i$ , yields
$$\boxed{|D\cap V_T|\le12+o_T+f_T\qquad(u_T\in D).}         \tag{6}$$
The additional adjacency from  $u_T$  to its distinguished  $y$ -vertex can only strengthen this bound.2.3. Every entire wing has cap  $20$ This bound holds whether or not  $u_T$  is selected:
$$\boxed{|D\cap V_T|\le20.}                                \tag{7}$$
In the distinguished block, partition its six vertices together with  $u_T$  into
$$\{a_0^T,x_0^T,c_0^T\}\cong P_3,
\qquad
\{y_0^T,b_0^T,i_0^T,u_T\}\cong C_4.$$
Both pieces have dissociation number two. Each of the other four blocks is a  $P_6$  and contributes at most four. Therefore
$$|D\cap V_T|\le2+2+4\cdot4=20.$$
Edges between pieces do not invalidate an upper bound obtained by summing their individual caps.3. The cap  $35$ We now separate the three possibilities for the two  $u$ -vertices.Case A: Neither  $u_L$  nor  $u_R$  is selectedBy (3),
$$|D|\le30+g_L+g_R.$$
It remains to prove
$$g_L+g_R\le5.                                            \tag{8}$$
Pair the ten block positions into the five slots
$$P_j=(L_j,R_{j+1}),\qquad j\in\mathbb Z/5\mathbb Z.$$
A slot contains zero, one, or two good blocks.Suppose  $P_j$  contains two good blocks. Because the two witness pairs are completely joined, neither block can contain a selected  $b$ -witness: such a  $b$  would have a selected cross neighbour, contradicting goodness. Thus the selected witnesses in these two blocks are exactly
$$a_j^L,\qquad a_{j+1}^R.$$
They are adjacent, so both are cross-saturated.Now: $a_j^L$  is adjacent to both witnesses of  $R_j$ , so  $R_j$  contains no selected witness. $a_{j+1}^R$  is adjacent to both witnesses of  $L_{j-1}$ , so  $L_{j-1}$  contains no selected witness.Hence the preceding slot
$$P_{j-1}=(L_{j-1},R_j)$$
contains no good block—in fact, no selected witness at all.Thus every double-good slot forces its predecessor to be empty. The predecessor map is injective, so the number of double-good slots is at most the number of empty slots. If these numbers are  $d_2,d_0$ , respectively, then
$$g_L+g_R=5+d_2-d_0\le5.$$
This proves (8), and therefore
$$|D|\le35.$$
Case B: Both  $u_L$  and  $u_R$  are selectedAgain use the five slots  $P_j=(L_j,R_{j+1})$ . In each slot,
$$o_j^L+f_j^L+o_{j+1}^R+f_{j+1}^R\le2.                   \tag{9}$$
If only one block is occupied, its contribution to the left side is at most two. If both are occupied, the complete  $K_{2,2}$  makes every selected witness in either block cross-saturated. Neither block can then be full and cross-free, so the contribution is exactly two.Summing (9),
$$o_L+o_R+f_L+f_R\le10.$$
Applying (6) in both wings gives the stronger bound
$$\boxed{|D|\le24+10=34.}                                 \tag{10}$$
Case C: Exactly one  $u$ -vertex is selectedFirst suppose
$$u_L\in D,\qquad u_R\notin D.$$
Let  $J\subseteq\mathbb Z/5\mathbb Z$  be the indices of good right blocks, and put  $r=|J|$ . By (3),
$$|D\cap V_R|\le15+r.                                     \tag{11}$$
We will show
$$|D\cap V_L|\le20-r.                                     \tag{12}$$
Write  $o=o_L$  and  $f=f_L$ .If  $r=0$ , (12) is precisely the universal wing cap (7).Suppose  $1\le r\le4$ . Two observations give the required bound.First,
$$o\le4.                                                  \tag{13}$$
For if every left block were occupied, a selected right witness  $a_k^R$  would have selected neighbours in both complete left blocks  $L_{k-1}$  and  $L_{k-2}$ , contradicting the dissociation condition. A selected  $b_k^R$  in a good block would have a selected neighbour in the complete left block  $L_{k-1}$ , contradicting its cross-isolation. Thus no right block could be good.Second,
$$f\le4-r.                                                \tag{14}$$
Any selected witness in right block  $R_k$  prevents both  $L_k$  and  $L_{k-1}$  from being full and cross-free: $a_k^L$  meets both witnesses of  $R_k$ ; $L_{k-1}$  and  $R_k$  have all four cross edges.Therefore
$$f\le5-|J\cup(J-1)|.$$
Every nonempty proper subset  $J$  of the five-cycle satisfies
$$|J\cup(J-1)|\ge|J|+1.$$
Otherwise  $J=J-1$ , and invariance under a cyclic shift would force  $J$  to be empty or the whole cycle. This proves (14).Now (6), (13), and (14) give
$$|D\cap V_L|
\le12+o+f
\le12+4+(4-r)
=20-r.$$
Finally suppose  $r=5$ . Every left block is excluded from being full and cross-free, so  $f=0$ . Also,
$$o\le3.                                                  \tag{15}$$
We already know  $o\ne5$ . If  $o=4$ , let  $L_h$  be the unique empty left block. For a right good block  $R_k$ :if  $a_k^R$  is selected, at least one of  $L_{k-1},L_{k-2}$  must be empty, so  $k\in\{h+1,h+2\}$ ;if  $b_k^R$  is selected, its cross-isolation requires  $L_{k-1}$  to be empty, so  $k=h+1$ .Thus at most two right block indices could be good, contradicting  $r=5$ . This proves (15), and (6) gives
$$|D\cap V_L|\le12+3=15=20-r.$$
Combining (11) and (12), the total is at most  $35$ .For completeness, when  $u_R$  is selected instead, the same counting uses these explicit index relations: $a_j^L$  meets both witnesses in each of  $R_j,R_{j+1}$ ; $b_j^L$  meets both witnesses in  $R_{j+1}$ ;any selected witness in  $L_j$  excludes full cross-free right blocks  $R_{j+1},R_{j+2}$ .These give the same bounds  $o\le4$ ,  $f\le4-r$  for  $1\le r\le4$ , and  $o\le3,f=0$  for  $r=5$ . In the last case, a unique empty right block  $R_h$  would permit good left indices only in  $\{h,h-1\}$ .All adjacencies used survive deletion of  $b_0^Lb_0^R$ .The three cases exhaust all dissociation sets, proving
$$\boxed{\beta_2(H^-)\le35.}                              \tag{16}$$
4. Attainment: both dissociation numbers equal  $35$ Your displayed set is
$$D_0=
\{c_j,x_j,i_j:0\le j\le4\}
\;\cup\;
\{x_j,y_j,a_j,b_j:5\le j\le9\}.$$
It has  $15+20=35$  vertices.In each left block it induces the edge  $c_jx_j$  and the isolated vertex  $i_j$ . In each right block it induces the two edges  $x_ja_j$  and  $y_jb_j$ . There are no selected left witnesses, and neither  $u$ -vertex is selected, so no further edges occur.Thus  $D_0$  is a dissociation set in both  $H^-$  and  $H$ . Since adding edges cannot increase the dissociation number,
$$35\le\beta_2(H)\le\beta_2(H^-)\le35.$$
Therefore
$$\boxed{\beta_2(H)=\beta_2(H-e)=35.}$$
5. The graph and selection satisfy the required hypothesesA bipartition is
$$A=
\{a_j,b_j,c_j:0\le j\le4\}
\cup
\{x_j,y_j,i_j:5\le j\le9\}
\cup\{u_L\},
\qquad B=V(H)\setminus A.$$
In  $H$ , the degrees are:VerticesDegreeEvery  $a_j,b_j$  $6$ Every  $c_j,x_j,i_j$  $2$  $y_0,y_5$  $3$ Other  $y_j$  $2$  $u_L,u_R$  $6$ For the right witnesses, the four baseline incoming indices are  $t,t-1,t-2,t-3$ , and an additional incoming index  $t-4$  occurs exactly for even  $t$ . Hence right  $a$ -witnesses have cross degree five and right  $b$ -witnesses cross degree four, just as on the left. Including their local edges gives degree six.Deleting  $e$  lowers only the degrees of  $b_0,b_5$ , from six to five.The specified selection
$$S=\{c_j,x_j,y_j,i_j:0\le j\le9\}$$
induces ten  $P_3$ 's and ten isolates. Formation is witnessed by
$$a_j-x_j-c_j,\qquad b_j-y_j-c_j,
\qquad u_L-y_0-c_0,\qquad u_R-y_5-c_5.$$
The literal deletion arguments are valid:Deleted vertexVertex that fails formationReason $x_j$  $a_j$ It has no selected neighbour. $y_j$  $b_j$ Its only selected neighbour is  $i_j$ , which has no selected neighbour. $c_j$  $a_j$ Its only selected neighbour is  $x_j$ , which has no selected neighbour. $i_j$  $i_j$ Both of its neighbours are outside the remaining selection.For an outside vertex to lie in a  $P_3$  with two selected vertices, it must either have two selected neighbours or have a selected neighbour with a further selected neighbour. Each row excludes both possibilities.Formation is upward closed in the selected set, so failure of every one-vertex deletion proves inclusion minimality. Changes involving only witness-to-witness edges preserve these arguments.6. Two-connectivity of  $H-e$ The witness edges of offsets  $2,3$  form a Hamiltonian cycle. Indeed,
$$\alpha_t\longrightarrow\beta_{t+3}\longrightarrow\alpha_{t+1}$$
uses those two offsets. Advancing  $t$  by one traverses all ten left and all ten right witnesses. The deleted edge has offset zero and is absent from this cycle.Starting from the cycle, add the following open ears:For each of the ten blocks,
$$a_j-x_j-c_j-y_j-b_j.$$
In the left wing,
$$b_0-i_0-u_L-i_1-b_1,$$
followed by
$$b_j-i_j-u_L,\qquad j=2,3,4.$$
In the right wing,
$$b_5-i_5-u_R-i_6-b_6,$$
followed by
$$b_j-i_j-u_R,\qquad j=7,8,9.$$
At each step the endpoints are distinct existing vertices and the internal vertices are new. Adding such an ear to a two-connected graph preserves two-connectivity: after any one vertex deletion, every surviving part of the ear remains attached to the surviving connected old graph.This constructs a spanning two-connected subgraph of  $H^-$ . Adding the unused witness edges and the two distinguished  $u$ -to- $y$  edges preserves two-connectivity. Hence  $H^-$  is two-connected.7. The cyclic family: no additional gapTake  $k$  disjoint copies  $H^-_r$ , with copy indices modulo  $k$ , and write
$$p_r=b_{0,r},\qquad q_r=b_{5,r}.$$
Add the edges
$$p_rq_{r+1}.$$
Call the result  $G_k$ .Each deleted degree slot is restored exactly once. The graph remains simple and bipartite, with minimum degree two and maximum degree six. For  $k=1$ , this simply restores  $e$ , giving  $H$ .Two-connectivityAfter deletion of any one vertex, each surviving base  $H^-_r$  remains connected. Because  $p_r\ne q_r$ , deleting one vertex destroys at most one linking edge.For  $k\ge3$ , the cycle of bases remains connected after removal of at most one link. For  $k=2$ , there are two distinct links between the bases and at least one survives. For  $k=1$ ,  $H$  contains the two-connected spanning graph  $H^-$ .Thus every  $G_k$  is two-connected.Exact dissociation numberAny dissociation set  $D$  of  $G_k$  restricts to a dissociation set in each  $H^-_r$ . Therefore
$$|D|
=\sum_r |D\cap V(H^-_r)|
\le35k.$$
Repeating  $D_0$  attains  $35k$ : every new linking edge has its left endpoint  $p_r=b_{0,r}$  outside the repeated set. Hence
$$\boxed{\beta_2(G_k)=35k.}$$
The repeated selection  $S_k$  has size  $40k$ , induces  $10k$  copies of  $P_3$  and  $10k$  isolates, and remains inclusion-minimal and forming. Consequently
$$\boxed{
|S_k|-\beta_2(G_k)
=5k
=\frac{5}{62}|V(G_k)|.
}$$
This attains the accepted degree bound exactly for every  $k\ge1$ . The conclusion concerns the displayed minimal selections and the unrestricted dissociation number; no exact SF value is needed or established.
